title: Book V: The Dead Hand — Chapter XLV
paragraphs:
It is the humor of many heads to extol the days of their forefathers,
and declaim against the wickedness of times present. Which
notwithstanding they cannot handsomely do, without the borrowed help
and satire of times past; condemning the vices of their own times, by
the expressions of vices in times which they commend, which cannot but
argue the community of vice in both. Horace, therefore, Juvenal, and
Persius, were no prophets, although their lines did seem to indigitate
and point at our times.—SIR THOMAS BROWNE: _Pseudodoxia Epidemica_.

Like other forms of opposition, the hostility to the New Fever Hospital which Lydgate had described to Dorothea could be viewed in many ways. To him it was a mixture of jealousy and thick-headed prejudice. Mr. Bulstrode saw professional jealousy too, but also a determination to frustrate him personally, prompted chiefly by hatred of the living religion he had tried to represent effectively as a layman. Certainly that hatred found excuses outside religion, excuses only too easily discovered in the tangled workings of human conduct. These might be called the administration's views. An opposition, however, has an unlimited supply of objections. It need never stop at the boundary of knowledge, but can draw endlessly on the vast territories of ignorance. Much of what Middlemarch said about the New Hospital and its management was certainly an echo, for heaven has taken care not to make everyone an original thinker. Yet there were differences reflecting every shade of society, from Dr. Minchin's polished restraint to the cutting declarations of Mrs. Dollop, landlady of the Tankard in Slaughter Lane.

The more Mrs. Dollop repeated her assertion, the more firmly she believed it: Dr. Lydgate meant to let patients die in the Hospital, if he didn't actually poison them, so that he could cut them up without asking anyone's permission. It was a known “fact” that he had wanted to cut up Mrs. Goby, as respectable a woman as any in Parley Street, who had money held in trust before she married. A poor story for a doctor! If he was any good, he ought to know what was wrong with you before you died, instead of poking about inside you afterwards. If that wasn't reason, Mrs. Dollop wanted to know what was. Her listeners generally felt her opinion was a defence: if it fell, there would be no end to cutting up bodies. Burke and Hare, with their pitch plasters, had shown that clearly enough. Middlemarch wanted none of that sort of business that ended on the gallows!

Do not suppose the opinions expressed at the Tankard in Slaughter Lane were unimportant to the medical profession. That venerable, genuine public house—the original Tankard, known as Dollop's—was the meeting place of a large mutual-benefit club. Some months earlier its members had voted on whether to dismiss their long-serving doctor, “Doctor Gambit,” in favour of “this Doctor Lydgate,” who could apparently perform astonishing cures and rescue people other practitioners had abandoned. Two members had tipped the vote against Lydgate. For private reasons they felt that the ability to revive people as good as dead was a doubtful recommendation, and might interfere with the favours of Providence. During the year, however, public feeling had changed, as the agreement at Dollop's now showed.

Well over a year earlier, before anyone knew anything about Lydgate's skill, judgments of it had naturally differed. They rested on a sense of probability located perhaps in the stomach or pineal gland. Though its verdicts varied, it remained a valuable guide where evidence was entirely absent. Patients with chronic illnesses, or lives worn thin like old Featherstone's, had immediately wanted to try him. Many people who disliked paying medical bills also welcomed the thought of opening an account with a new doctor. They could send for him freely whenever the children's temper needed a dose, occasions on which the established practitioners often became grumpy. Everyone inclined to employ Lydgate considered him likely to be clever. Some thought he might be better than the others “where the liver was concerned.” At least a few bottles of his “stuff” could do no harm. If they proved useless, one could return to the Purifying Pills, which kept you alive even if they failed to remove the yellowness. But these were relatively unimportant people. Respectable Middlemarch families would naturally not change doctors without a demonstrated reason. Nor did everyone who had employed Mr. Peacock feel obliged to accept a stranger simply because he was Peacock's successor. They objected that he was “unlikely to be as good as Peacock.”

Before long, however, enough details about Lydgate had circulated to produce more specific expectations and turn differences of opinion into partisanship. Some were those impressive facts whose significance is entirely concealed, like a statistical total without any standard of comparison but with an exclamation mark after it. Think what shudders the cubic feet of oxygen swallowed yearly by an adult man might have caused in certain Middlemarch circles! “Oxygen! Nobody knows what that is. Is it any wonder cholera has reached Dantzic? And yet some people claim quarantine does no good!”

One early rumour was that Lydgate did not dispense medicines. This offended both the physicians, whose exclusive distinction seemed threatened, and the surgeon-apothecaries, among whom he counted himself. Only a short time earlier, they might have expected the law to support them against a man who, without claiming a London M.D., dared to charge for anything except drugs. But Lydgate lacked the experience to foresee that his new practice would offend the public even more. Mr. Mawmsey, an important grocer in the Top Market, was not his patient, but questioned him pleasantly about it. Lydgate unwisely gave a quick explanation for the ordinary listener. He pointed out that if practitioners could earn their living only by presenting long bills for draughts, pills and mixtures, their professional character must suffer and the public would be continually harmed.

“That's how hardworking doctors can become almost as harmful as quacks,” Lydgate said rather carelessly. “To earn their bread, they have to overdose the king's subjects. That's a bad kind of treason, Mr. Mawmsey: fatally undermining the constitution.”

Mr. Mawmsey was an overseer of the poor, and his interview with Lydgate concerned relief paid outside the workhouse. He also had asthma and a growing family. He was therefore important medically as well as in his own estimation. Indeed, he was an exceptional grocer, with hair arranged in a flame-shaped pyramid and a shopkeeper's deference of the warm, encouraging kind. His compliments were jocular; he considerately refrained from unleashing the full force of his intellect. His friendly joking questions had set the tone of Lydgate's answer. But let the wise beware of explaining too readily. It multiplies the opportunities for error, lengthening a sum for people certain to miscalculate.

As Lydgate finished, he smiled and put his foot in the stirrup. Mr. Mawmsey laughed more than he would have if he had understood the doctor's reference to the king's subjects, and repeated, “Good morning, sir, good morning,” with the air of someone who saw the whole matter clearly. In fact, he was disturbed. For years he had paid precisely itemised bills, certain that every half-crown and eighteenpence represented something measurable delivered to him. He had done so contentedly as part of his duties as husband and father, seeing an unusually long bill as a distinction worth mentioning. Besides the substantial benefit the medicines brought to “self and family,” he enjoyed making shrewd assessments of their immediate effects and reporting intelligently to guide Mr. Gambit. This practitioner stood just below Wrench or Toller and was especially valued for attending childbirth. Mr. Mawmsey thought very little of his abilities in any other field, but in doctoring, he liked to say confidentially, he put Gambit above them all.

These were weightier reasons than a newcomer's superficial talk. That talk seemed flimsier still when repeated in the drawing room above the shop to Mrs. Mawmsey. A prolific mother, she was accustomed to being fussed over. Mr. Gambit attended her more or less frequently, and occasional attacks required Dr. Minchin.

“Does this Mr. Lydgate mean that taking medicine does no good?” asked Mrs. Mawmsey, who tended to drawl. “I'd like him to explain how I could get through Fair time without taking strengthening medicine for a month beforehand. Think what I have to provide for customers who call, my dear!” She turned to a close woman friend sitting nearby. “A big veal pie, a stuffed fillet, a round of beef, ham, tongue, and so on and so on! But it's the pink mixture that keeps me going best, not the brown. Mr. Mawmsey, I'm surprised that someone with _your_ experience could bear to listen. I'd have told him straight away that I knew better.”

“No, no, no,” Mr. Mawmsey replied. “I wasn't going to give him my opinion. My motto is: hear everything and judge for yourself. But he didn't know whom he was talking to. _He_ wasn't going to twist me around his finger. People often offer to teach me things when they might as well say, ‘Mawmsey, you're a fool.’ I simply smile. I humour everyone's little weakness. If medicine had harmed self and family, I'd have discovered it by now.”
The following day, Mr. Gambit heard that Lydgate was going about saying medicine was useless.
“Really!” he said, raising his eyebrows in guarded surprise. He was a stout, rough-voiced man with a large ring on his fourth finger. “Then how does he intend to cure his patients?”

“That's exactly what I say,” answered Mrs. Mawmsey, who habitually added force to her remarks by leaning heavily on the pronouns. “Does _he_ imagine people will pay just for him to sit with them and then leave?”

Mr. Gambit had spent a great deal of time sitting with Mrs. Mawmsey, giving detailed accounts of his own bodily habits and other concerns. Naturally he knew she intended no insinuation, since he had never charged for his spare time or personal stories. He answered jokingly:
“Well, you know, Lydgate is a handsome young man.”
“_I_ certainly wouldn't employ him,” said Mrs. Mawmsey. “_Other people_ can do as they like.”

Mr. Gambit could thus leave the leading grocer's house without fearing competition. He did, however, feel that Lydgate belonged to that class of hypocrites who advertise their own honesty to discredit other people. It might be worth someone's while to expose him. Yet Gambit's practice was satisfactory, rich in the smells of retail businesses which suggested that payments could be settled by balancing accounts. He thought it not worth exposing Lydgate until he knew how. His education was limited, and he had worked his way up against considerable professional contempt. But pronouncing the breathing organs “longs” made him no worse at delivering babies.

Other doctors felt better equipped. Mr. Toller shared the town's best practice and belonged to an old Middlemarch family. There were Tollers in law and every other occupation above retail trade. Unlike our irritable friend Wrench, he took apparent provocations with perfect ease. He was a well-bred man of quiet humour, kept a comfortable house, enjoyed a little sport when he could, was close to Mr. Hawley and hostile to Mr. Bulstrode. It may seem strange that someone with such pleasant habits should favour heroic treatment: bleeding, blistering and starving his patients with an impartial disregard for his own example. Yet the contrast enhanced his patients' opinion of his ability. They often remarked that his manner might be lazy, but his treatment was as vigorous as anyone could wish. Nobody took his profession more seriously, they said. He might be slow to arrive, but once he came, he _did_ something. He was much liked in his circle, and his casual irony gave twice the force to anything he implied against another person.

Naturally he tired of smiling and saying “Ah!” whenever he heard that Mr. Peacock's successor did not intend to dispense medicines. When Mr. Hackbutt mentioned it over the wine at a dinner party, Toller laughed and said, “Then Dibbitts will clear out his stale drugs. I like little Dibbitts. I'm pleased he's in luck.”

“I take your point, Toller,” said Mr. Hackbutt, “and entirely agree. I shall find an opportunity to say so. A doctor should answer for the quality of the medicines his patients consume. That is the reasoning behind the established system of charging. Nothing is more objectionable than parading reform when there is no actual improvement.”

“Parading it, Hackbutt?” Toller asked ironically. “I don't see how. A man can hardly parade something nobody believes in. There's no reform involved. The question is whether the doctor gets his profit on medicines from the chemist or from the patient, and whether there's an additional fee called attendance.”
“Exactly. Another damned new version of the old humbug,” said Mr. Hawley, handing the decanter to Mr. Wrench.
Usually restrained in his drinking, Mr. Wrench often took wine rather freely at parties and became more irritable as a result.

“‘Humbug’ is easy enough to throw around, Hawley,” he said. “What I object to is doctors fouling their own nest, raising an outcry across the country as if a general practitioner who dispenses medicine couldn't be a gentleman. I reject that accusation with contempt. The most ungentlemanly trick a man can play is to enter his profession with innovations that slander his colleagues' time-honoured methods. That's my opinion, and I'm prepared to defend it against anyone who disagrees.” Mr. Wrench's voice had grown extremely sharp.
“I can't oblige you by disagreeing, Wrench,” said Mr. Hawley, pushing his hands into his trouser pockets.

“My dear fellow,” Mr. Toller interposed soothingly, looking at Wrench, “the physicians have had their toes trodden on more than we have. If it's a matter of dignity, Minchin and Sprague are the ones to ask.”
“Does medical law offer no remedy against these encroachments?” Mr. Hackbutt asked, generously wishing to contribute his expertise. “What's the legal position, Hawley?”
“Nothing to be done legally,” Hawley replied. “I examined it for Sprague. You'd only smash your nose against some damned judge's ruling.”
“Nonsense, no need for law,” said Toller. “In practical terms, the attempt is ridiculous. Patients won't like it—certainly not Peacock's, who've been accustomed to being drained. Pass the wine.”

Toller's prediction proved partly correct. If the Mawmseys, who had no intention of employing Lydgate, were troubled by his supposed attack on medicine, his patients would inevitably watch with some anxiety to see whether he used every available means of treatment. Even kind Mr. Powderell, whose consistently charitable interpretations inclined him to respect Lydgate's apparent conscientious search for a better method, became doubtful during his wife's attack of erysipelas. He could not help mentioning that on a similar occasion Mr. Peacock had prescribed a series of pills. He could describe them only by their remarkable success in restoring Mrs. Powderell before Michaelmas from an illness that had begun in an unusually hot August. Finally, torn between not wanting to hurt Lydgate and fearing the omission of any “means,” he persuaded his wife secretly to take Widgeon's Purifying Pills. This respected Middlemarch remedy supposedly checked every disease at its source by acting immediately on the blood. They were not to tell Lydgate about this additional treatment. Mr. Powderell himself had no firm confidence in it, only a hope that it might carry a blessing.

At this uncertain stage of his arrival, however, Lydgate benefited from what we mortals rashly call good fortune. I suppose no new doctor ever settled anywhere without surprising someone with a cure. Such cures are fortune's testimonials, deserving as much credit as written or printed ones. Various patients recovered under Lydgate's care, some from dangerous illnesses. People remarked that the new doctor and his new methods at least had the merit of bringing patients back from death's door. The nonsense spoken on these occasions irritated Lydgate all the more because it gave him exactly the prestige an incompetent, unscrupulous man would want. The other doctors, simmering with dislike, would surely take it as evidence that he encouraged ignorant publicity. But even his proud frankness was restrained by the recognition that fighting ignorant interpretations was as useless as whipping fog. And “good fortune” insisted on employing them.

Mrs. Larcher had just begun taking a charitable interest in her cleaning woman's alarming symptoms when Dr. Minchin called. She asked him to examine the woman immediately and provide a certificate for the Infirmary. After examining her, he described the case in writing as a tumour and recommended that the bearer, Nancy Nash, be treated as an outpatient. On her way there, Nancy stopped at home and let the corset maker and his wife, whose attic she rented, read the doctor's paper. She consequently became a subject of sympathetic discussion in the neighbouring shops of Churchyard Lane. At first the tumour was said to be as large and hard as a duck's egg; later that day it had grown to the size of “your fist.” Most listeners agreed it would have to be cut out. But one knew oil, and another “squitchineal,” to be capable of softening and reducing any internal lump if enough was swallowed: oil by gradually making it supple, squitchineal by eating it away.

Meanwhile, Nancy reached the Infirmary on one of Lydgate's days there. After questioning and examining her, he told the resident surgeon quietly, “It isn't a tumour. It's cramp.” He prescribed a blistering treatment and an iron mixture and told her to rest at home. He also gave her a note for Mrs. Larcher, whom Nancy called her best employer, confirming that she needed nourishing food.

Before long Nancy became alarmingly worse in her attic. The supposed tumour had indeed yielded to the blister, but only by moving elsewhere and causing fiercer pain. The corset maker's wife fetched Lydgate. He visited Nancy at home for a fortnight, until his treatment restored her completely and she returned to work. Yet Churchyard Lane and other streets still called it a tumour, as did Mrs. Larcher herself. When Lydgate's remarkable cure was mentioned to Dr. Minchin, he naturally disliked saying, “It wasn't a tumour; I was wrong to call it that.” Instead he replied, “Really! Ah, I recognised a surgical case, not a fatal one.” Privately, however, he had been annoyed when he asked at the Infirmary about the woman he had referred two days earlier. The resident surgeon, a young man pleased to irritate Minchin without consequences, had told him exactly what happened. Minchin privately judged it improper for a general practitioner to contradict a physician's diagnosis so openly. Later he agreed with Wrench that Lydgate showed an unpleasant disregard for professional etiquette. Lydgate did not use the episode as a reason to admire himself or especially despise Minchin: equally qualified men often corrected one another's errors. But gossip took up this astonishing tumour, scarcely distinguished from cancer and considered more dreadful because it wandered. The proof of Lydgate's marvellous skill overcame much prejudice against his approach to medicines. Had he not rapidly restored Nancy Nash after she had rolled and rolled in agony from a hard, stubborn tumour that had nevertheless been forced to yield?

What could Lydgate do? When a lady is expressing amazement at your skill, telling her she is entirely mistaken and rather foolish is offensive. Explaining the nature of diseases would only add to his breaches of medical decorum. So he had to wince at the prospect of success founded on ignorant praise that overlooked every genuine merit.

With a more prominent patient, Mr. Borthrop Trumbull, Lydgate knew he had proved himself better than an ordinary doctor, though here too his advantage was doubtful. The eloquent auctioneer developed pneumonia. As a former patient of Mr. Peacock, he sent for Lydgate, whom he had already announced he intended to patronise. Mr. Trumbull was robust and therefore a good subject for the expectant method: observing the progress of an interesting illness while leaving it as far as possible to itself, recording its stages for future guidance. From the way he described his sensations, Lydgate guessed he would like to share his doctor's confidence and regard himself as a partner in the cure. Without much surprise, the auctioneer learned that his constitution, carefully watched, could be left to its own resources. It would offer a beautiful example of the disease with every phase clearly displayed. He probably possessed the rare mental strength to submit willingly to a trial of rational treatment, making the disorder of his lungs a benefit to society at large.
Mr. Trumbull agreed immediately, warmly adopting the view that an illness of his offered medical science no ordinary opportunity.

“Have no fear, sir. You're not addressing someone entirely ignorant of the _vis medicatrix_,” he said. His usual elevated manner sounded rather pathetic through his difficulty in breathing. He faced the absence of medicine without flinching. He was greatly supported by the thermometer's use, which implied the importance of his temperature; by knowing that he supplied specimens for the microscope; and by learning new words worthy of the dignity of his secretions. Lydgate was perceptive enough to indulge him in a little technical conversation.

It is easy to imagine Mr. Trumbull getting out of bed eager to discuss an illness that had demonstrated the strength of his mind as well as his body. Nor was he slow to praise the doctor who had recognised the quality of his patient. The auctioneer was not ungenerous. He enjoyed giving others their due, feeling he could afford it. He had picked up “expectant method” and rang changes on this and other learned phrases while declaring that Lydgate “knew a thing or two more than the other doctors—was far more deeply acquainted with the secrets of his profession than most of his colleagues.”

All this preceded Fred Vincy's illness, which gave Wrench's hostility a more definite personal basis. The newcomer already threatened to become an annoying rival. He was certainly annoying as a practical criticism of older, hard-pressed doctors who had had other things to do than concern themselves with untested ideas. His practice had expanded in a few directions. From the beginning, reports of his distinguished family had brought invitations everywhere, obliging the other doctors to meet him at dinner in the best houses. Being forced into company with someone you dislike does not invariably produce mutual affection. Rarely had they agreed so completely as in calling Lydgate arrogant, yet ready to crawl before Bulstrode in hopes of eventually dominating everyone himself. Mr. Farebrother, whose name was a leading banner for the anti-Bulstrode party, consistently defended and befriended him. This was attributed to Farebrother's inexplicable habit of fighting on both sides.

The ground was therefore thoroughly prepared for an outbreak of professional disgust when Bulstrode announced his rules for the New Hospital. They were especially infuriating because nobody could presently interfere with his wishes. Everyone except Lord Medlicote had refused to help finance the building, saying they preferred supporting the Old Infirmary. Bulstrode paid every expense. He had ceased regretting that he was buying the right to carry out his improvements without prejudiced colleagues obstructing him. But the sums were large and construction had dragged on. Caleb Garth had undertaken it, suffered business failure while it was in progress, and withdrawn from managing the business before the interior fittings began. Speaking of the Hospital, Caleb often said that whatever sort of metal Bulstrode might prove when tested, he liked sound carpentry and masonry and understood drains and chimneys. The Hospital had in fact become intensely important to Bulstrode. He would willingly have continued to pay a large annual sum to rule it without a board. But another cherished aim also needed money: he wanted to buy land near Middlemarch. He therefore hoped for substantial contributions to the Hospital's running costs. Meanwhile he drew up his system of management. The Hospital would treat fever in all its forms exclusively. Lydgate would be chief medical superintendent, free to conduct the comparative investigations whose importance his studies, especially in Paris, had revealed to him. Other visiting doctors could advise, but could not overrule his final decisions. General management would belong solely to five directors associated with Bulstrode, their voting strength proportional to their contributions. The board would fill its own vacancies. No crowd of small subscribers would have a share in governing it.
Every doctor in the town immediately refused to serve as a visiting physician at the Fever Hospital.

“Very well,” Lydgate told Bulstrode. “Our resident surgeon and dispenser is excellent, clear-headed and skilful with his hands. We'll get Webbe from Crabsley to come twice a week. He's as good a country practitioner as any of them. Protheroe can come from Brassing for any unusual operation. I'll simply have to work harder. I've given up my post at the Infirmary. The project will succeed despite them, and then they'll be glad to join us. Things can't continue as they are. There'll soon have to be reforms of every kind, and then young men may be glad to study here.” He was in high spirits.

“You can rely on me not to draw back, Mr. Lydgate,” said Bulstrode. “As long as I see you vigorously pursuing high purposes, my support will be constant. I humbly trust that the blessing which has accompanied my efforts against this town's spirit of evil will continue. I have no doubt I can find suitable directors to assist me. Mr. Brooke of Tipton has already agreed and promised an annual contribution. He hasn't named the amount—probably it won't be large. But he will be a useful board member.”
A useful member might perhaps mean someone who would propose nothing and always vote with Mr. Bulstrode.

The doctors scarcely concealed their dislike of Lydgate now. Neither Dr. Sprague nor Dr. Minchin said they objected to his knowledge or desire to improve treatment. They objected to his arrogance, which nobody could wholly deny. They suggested that he was insolent and pretentious, addicted to the reckless innovation for noise and display that defined a charlatan.

Once the word “charlatan” was in circulation, nobody would let it drop. At that time the world was excited by Mr. St. John Long's miraculous performances. “Noblemen and gentlemen” testified that he had drawn a mercury-like fluid from a patient's temples.
One day Mr. Toller remarked to Mrs. Taft with a smile, “Bulstrode has found his match in Lydgate. A religious charlatan is bound to appreciate charlatans of other kinds.”

“Yes, indeed, I can well imagine,” Mrs. Taft replied, carefully keeping her count of thirty stitches in mind. “There are so many of them. I remember Mr. Cheshire and his irons, trying to straighten people whom the Almighty had made crooked.”

“No, no,” said Toller. “Cheshire was perfectly respectable, quite open and honest. St. John Long is the sort of man we call a charlatan: advertising cures by methods nobody understands, drawing attention to himself by pretending to penetrate deeper than other people. The other day he pretended to tap a man's brain and draw mercury from it.”
“Good heavens! What dreadful tampering with people's constitutions!” exclaimed Mrs. Taft.

After that, people in various quarters believed Lydgate experimented on even respectable constitutions for his own ends. How much more likely, then, that his irresponsible experiments would make a complete mess of hospital patients! Above all, as the Tankard's landlady had said, he could be expected to cut up their dead bodies without a thought. Lydgate had attended Mrs. Goby, who apparently died of a heart condition whose symptoms had been unclear. Too boldly, he had asked her relatives for permission to open the body. The offence spread quickly beyond Parley Street, where she had long lived on an income substantial enough to make any association of her body with Burke and Hare's victims a flagrant insult to her memory.

This was the state of affairs when Lydgate spoke to Dorothea about the Hospital. As we see, he met hostility and foolish misunderstanding with considerable spirit, knowing his own measure of success had helped provoke them.

“They won't drive me out,” he said in a confidential conversation in Mr. Farebrother's study. “I've got a good opportunity here to pursue what matters most to me, and I'm fairly sure I can earn enough for our needs. Before long I shall be working as quietly as possible. Nothing tempts me away from home and work now. And I'm increasingly convinced it will be possible to show that all tissues have the same origin. Raspail and others are following the same line, and I've been losing time.”
“I can't predict anything about that,” said Farebrother, who had been thoughtfully smoking his pipe as Lydgate spoke. “But you'll survive the town's hostility if you're careful.”

“What does being careful mean?” Lydgate asked. “I simply do the work in front of me. I can no more prevent people's ignorance and malice than Vesalius could. You can't adjust your behaviour to foolish conclusions nobody could foresee.”

“Quite right. That wasn't what I meant. I meant only two things. First, keep as independent of Bulstrode as possible. Naturally you can continue your own good work with his help, but don't become tied to him. Perhaps that sounds like personal feeling on my part, and I admit there's plenty of it. But personal feeling isn't always wrong when you reduce it to the impressions that make it simply an opinion.”

“Bulstrode means nothing to me except in public matters,” Lydgate replied casually. “I'm not fond enough of him to become closely attached. But what was your second point?” He was holding his leg in the most comfortable position and felt little need for advice.

“This: be careful—_experto crede_, trust someone who knows—not to get tangled up over money. Something you let slip one day told me you disapprove of how much I play cards for money. You're quite right. But try to avoid needing little sums you haven't got. Perhaps this advice is unnecessary. Still, a man likes to pretend he's risen above himself by displaying his own bad example and preaching about it.”

Lydgate received these hints warmly, though he would hardly have tolerated them from anyone else. He could not help remembering his recent debts. But they had seemed unavoidable, and he now intended only to keep a modest household. The furniture he owed for would not need replacing, nor would his wine supply for a long time.

Many thoughts encouraged him then, and rightly. A man who knows he is devoted to worthy aims can endure petty hostility by remembering great workers who fought their way forward and suffered wounds. They hover in his mind like patron saints, giving invisible help. Back at home that evening after his conversation with Farebrother, Lydgate stretched his long legs on the sofa, leaned his head back, and clasped his hands behind it in his favourite thinking posture. Rosamond sat at the piano, playing tune after tune. All her husband knew about them—emotional elephant that he was—was that they suited his mood like musical sea breezes.

Something in Lydgate's appearance just then was very fine. Anyone might have felt encouraged to wager on his success. His dark eyes, mouth and forehead had the calm that comes from the fullness of contemplative thought: a mind no longer searching but seeing, and a gaze seemingly filled by what lies behind it.
After a while Rosamond left the piano and sat on a chair beside the sofa, facing her husband.
“Have you had enough music, my lord?” she asked, folding her hands before her with a little air of submission.

“Yes, darling, if you're tired,” Lydgate said gently. He turned his eyes towards her and let them rest there, but otherwise did not move. At that moment her presence perhaps added no more than a spoonful to a lake, and her feminine instinct was quick to detect it.
“What's occupying you so completely?” she asked, leaning forward until her face was nearer his.
He brought his hands down and rested them gently behind her shoulders.
“I'm thinking of a great man who, three hundred years ago, was about my age and had already opened a new era in anatomy.”
“I can't guess who,” Rosamond said, shaking her head. “We played guessing games about historical figures at Mrs. Lemon's, but never anatomists.”
“I'll tell you. He was called Vesalius. The only way he could learn anatomy so thoroughly was to steal bodies at night from graveyards and execution grounds.”
“Oh!” Disgust crossed Rosamond's pretty face. “I'm very glad you aren't Vesalius. Surely he could have found some less horrible way.”

“No, he couldn't,” said Lydgate, too absorbed to pay much attention to her response. “To obtain a complete skeleton, he had to steal a criminal's bleached bones from the gallows, bury them, then secretly carry them away bit by bit in the middle of the night.”

“I hope he isn't one of your great heroes,” Rosamond said, half joking and half anxious. “Otherwise you'll be getting up at night to visit St. Peter's churchyard. Remember how angry you said people were about Mrs. Goby. You have quite enough enemies already.”

“So did Vesalius, Rosy. No wonder Middlemarch's medical old fogies are jealous. Some of the greatest doctors alive attacked Vesalius furiously because they believed Galen, and he proved Galen wrong. They called him a liar and a poisonous monster. But the facts of the human body supported him, so he defeated them.”
“What became of him afterwards?” Rosamond asked, somewhat interested.

“He had plenty of fighting to do right to the end. At one point they angered him so much that he burned a large amount of his work. Then he was shipwrecked on his way from Jerusalem to take an important professorship at Padua. His death was rather miserable.”
After a brief silence, Rosamond said, “You know, Tertius, I often wish you weren't a doctor.”
“No, Rosy, don't say that,” said Lydgate, drawing her closer. “It's like saying you wish you'd married someone else.”
“Not at all. You're clever enough to do anything. You could easily have chosen something else. And all your cousins at Quallingham think your choice of profession puts you below them.”
“My cousins at Quallingham can go to the devil!” Lydgate exclaimed contemptuously. “It was just like their impertinence if they said anything of the kind to you.”
“Still, darling, I _don't_ think it's a pleasant profession,” said Rosamond. As we know, she could maintain an opinion with considerable quiet persistence.

“It's the noblest profession in the world, Rosamond,” Lydgate said seriously. “To say you love me without loving the doctor in me is like saying you enjoy eating a peach but dislike its flavour. Please don't say it again, darling. It hurts.”

“Very well, Doctor Solemn-face,” said Rosy, dimpling. “From now on I'll declare that I adore skeletons, body-snatchers, little bits in bottles, and quarrels with everyone that end in your dying miserably.”
“No, no, it isn't as bad as that,” said Lydgate. He abandoned his protest and resigned himself to caressing her.
